newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seen curbing strong dlr stance in 2nd term.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seen curbing strong dlr stance in 2nd term.

text.p: If President Bill Clinton is re-elected, his administration would likely moderate its longstanding strong-dollar policy within the coming year, experts said on Thursday.
And a reversal would be even more likely if the Democratic party also wins control of the House, they added.
"There is a good chance you will see a shift in their attitude; not right away, but in the course of the next year," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan and Co Inc.

Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd, said while an immediate policy shift after the election was unlikely, there was "great potential" of such a move occurring over the ensuing year.

The dollar appreciation in the run-up to the November 5 presidential election benefitted the incumbent as it buoyed stocks and bonds by encouraging foreign investment, said Chris Iggo, international economist at BZW/Barclays Bank in New York.
Leven added that the weak yen relative to the dollar aided the balance sheets of troubled Japanese banks, helping Clinton to avert a possible global financial crisis.

Recent criticism from major manufacturing companies hurt by a strong dollar, which makes U.S. exports less competitive, was of minor concern to Clinton-the-candidate, as the majority of such companies are primarily supporters of the Republican party, Leven said.

Organized labor, a critical well of support for Clinton, has stayed virtually silent about the dollar's steady rise and will only voice concern if a strong dollar causes a gain in the unemployment rate, experts said.
Any significant rise in joblessness has yet to occur as September unemployment was a lowly 5.2 percent, which economists forecasted held true in October as well.

"There were reasons why the administration might have changed its view, but they weren't pressing enough to change its stance ahead of the election ... After the election is a different story," said Iggo.
The most obvious catalyst for a change in official dollar policy would be if there is a worsening in the U.S. bilateral trade deficit with Japan.
While not widening, the bilateral deficit has held virtually steady over the past three to four months after a previous stretch of improvement, Iggo said.
Another catalyst would be if dollar/yen rose to a level that was not necessarily in the best interests of Japan.
"It is not a no-cost strategy to keep pushing the dollar higher for Japan," Leven said. "Honda has already said it might ship production out of U.S. plants and into Japan."

Honda Motor Co Ltd last Thursday said it was considering moving production of one of its popular estate car models back to Japan from the United States. The move would mark the first time a Japanese automaker has transferred production from an overseas base to Japan.

Malpede said the United States may need to depreciate the dollar against the yen in the near future to force Japan to stimulate its dragging economy from the fiscal side rather than to rely heavily on a weak yen.

Unsubstantiated market rumors of Japanese officials' discontent with current yen weakness against the greenback have become commonplace, hinting the market looks for Japan to change tack and not support dollar/yen at this high level.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, last Thursday denied market rumors that he had said the dollar's recent rise was too rapid.
In the final days of campaign 1996, the Clinton camp broke with precedent and was unusually supportive of the dollar despite its relatively high valuation against other leading currencies.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, the administration's point man for dollar policy, on Tuesday surprised the Asian currency markets when, in an interview with CNN, he discussed the reduced American budget deficit and forecast "a higher dollar coming out of this."

The remark, which departed from Rubin's familiar theme that a strong, not stronger, dollar is in the United States' best interest, sparked a dollar rally to a three-and-a-half-year high against the yen, dealers said.
